title: Supabase: what it is, pricing, MCP and RLS security (2026)
text:
Supabase in 2026: Postgres, auth and storage. Pricing as of Nov 11 (Free, Pro $25, Team $599), costs by stage, the MCP server and an RLS checklist before launch. 

Supabase is an open source backend platform built on PostgreSQL. Every Supabase project gets its own Postgres database, plus authentication, file storage, Edge Functions, realtime and vector search. As of November 11, 2026, the Free plan costs $0 (500 MB database, 50,000 monthly active users), the Pro plan starts at $25 per month and the Team plan at $599 per month.

...

All prices come from the official Supabase pricing page, checked on November 11, 2026.

In the same announcement, Supabase shared three figures: database launches grew 600% in one year, nearly 10 million developers build on the platform, and more than 60% of new databases come from an AI tool. The company credits Claude Code and Codex as growth drivers since January 2026.

## Supabase pricing in 2026: Free, Pro, Team and Enterprise

Supabase bills a subscription per organization, plus compute for each project and any usage beyond the quotas. Prices are in US dollars. Supabase applies VAT based on your billing address.

| Plan | Price | Active users included | Database | File storage | Backups | Pausing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Free | $0 | 50,000 | 500 MB | 1 GB | none | after 7 days of inactivity |
| Pro | from $25/month | 100,000, then $0.00325/MAU | 8 GB, then $0.125/GB | 100 GB, then $0.0213/GB | 7 days | never |
| Team | from $599/month | 100,000, then $0.00325/MAU | 8 GB, then $0.125/GB | 100 GB, then $0.0213/GB | 14 days | never |
| Enterprise | custom quote | custom | custom | custom | custom | never |

### Pro at $25 per month with $10 in compute credit

The Pro plan costs $25 per month and includes your first project. It adds 250 GB of egress (then $0.09/GB), 7 days of logs and email support. Every paid plan gets $10 of compute credit per month, which covers a Micro instance. Each additional project costs at least $10 per month.

...

### Compute pricing by instance size

Each project runs on its own Postgres instance, billed hourly. You can change the size at any time in the dashboard:

| Size | Monthly price | CPU | Memory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Micro | $10 | shared | 1 GB |
| Small | $15 | shared | 2 GB |
| Medium | $60 | shared | 4 GB |
| Large | $110 | 2 dedicated vCPUs | 8 GB |
| XL | $210 | 4 dedicated vCPUs | 16 GB |
| 16XL | $3,730 | 64 dedicated vCPUs | 256 GB |

You pay $25 for the Pro subscription, then the instance size of each project. Supabase deducts the $10 credit from any size.

### The spend cap, on by default

On the Pro plan, Supabase turns on a spend cap by default: you pay nothing for usage beyond the quotas. To go past 100,000 MAU or 250 GB of egress, turn it off in the dashboard.

### First users in production

As soon as paying customers depend on the app, move to Pro: no pausing, and 7 days of backups. Supabase deducts the $10 credit from the price of the Micro instance, so the total stays at $25. A development project alongside production adds $10.

title: Supabase Pricing: The Spend Cap Risk No Roundup Explains
text:
$0.00325. That is the exact price of one extra monthly active user on Supabase's Pro plan, once you cross the 100,000 included in the $25 base fee, according to Supabase's own pricing page. It is such a small number that most Supabase pricing breakdowns treat it as a footnote and move on to the next line item.

...

Tip

TL;DR: Supabase's Pro plan starts at $25 a month and includes a database, storage, bandwidth, and user quota, plus a $10 compute credit. Past those quotas, the platform's default "spend cap" does not bill you for the overage, it blocks the specific item that went over, like new signups or file uploads, until the next billing cycle. Supabase's own documentation confirms there is no built-in alert when that happens. Turning the spend cap off removes the block but replaces it with open-ended, unmonitored billing.

...

Supabase runs four tiers: Free, Pro, Team, and Enterprise. Supabase's pricing page lists the Free plan at $0 with a 500 MB database, 1 GB of file storage, 5 GB of egress, and 50,000 monthly active users, capped at two active projects that pause after a week of inactivity.

Pro starts at $25 a month per project. It raises every one of those ceilings: an 8 GB database, 100 GB of file storage, 250 GB of egress, and 100,000 monthly active users, and it stops the inactivity pause entirely. Team starts at $599 a month per organization and adds compliance features like SOC 2 and ISO 27001 support on top of the same usage quotas as Pro. Enterprise pricing is custom and negotiated directly with Supabase's sales team.

Every one of those included amounts has a published overage rate once you exceed it: $0.125 per extra GB of database, $0.0213 per extra GB of storage, $0.09 per extra GB of egress, and the $0.00325 per extra monthly active user mentioned above. On paper, that reads like a normal usage-based pricing model. The part that changes the story is what decides whether those overage rates ever actually get charged.

...

The $25 plan fee does not include the compute instance that runs your Postgres database. That is billed as its own line item, starting at the Micro tier.

Supabase's pricing page lists ten compute sizes: Micro at $10 a month with 1 GB of RAM, up through 16XL at $3,730 a month with 256 GB of RAM. Pro and Team plans both include a $10 monthly compute credit, which is subtracted from whichever tier you run, so Micro effectively costs nothing extra and moving up to Small only costs the $5 difference between its $15 price and the credit.

...

The other setting is to turn the spend cap off. Supabase's documentation states that with the cap disabled, the project keeps running past every quota and "any additional usage will be charged based on the item's cost per unit, as outlined on the pricing page." New signups keep working. File uploads keep working. The bill keeps growing, at the same per-unit rates listed above, for as long as nobody is watching the usage page.

title: Supabase Growth Story
text:
Supabase's growth after the Series A was driven by cadence, not a single viral moment. The Series B announcement disclosed an $80 million raise, bringing total funding to $116 million, with the platform now past 150,000 PostgreSQL databases and more than 110,000 developers. That round closed in May 2022 while the company was still shipping new product surfaces on a public schedule rather than behind closed doors.

...

Supabase monetizes through a metered freemium structure rather than a flat per-seat license. Per Supabase's own pricing page, the Free plan includes 50,000 monthly active users, 500 MB of database storage, 5 GB of egress, 1 GB of file storage, and 500,000 Edge Function invocations per month. The Pro plan, at $25 per month, raises those limits to 100,000 monthly active users, 8 GB of disk per project, 250 GB of egress, and 100 GB of file storage, with 2 million Edge Function invocations. A Team plan starts from $599 per month for organizations that need it.

That structure creates predictable scaling cliffs that buyers should plan for before they hit them. Egress overages on the Pro plan run $0.09 per gigabyte beyond the included allowance, a cost that compounds quickly for media-heavy applications. Authentication costs follow a similar pattern: adding another 500,000 monthly active users beyond the included quota adds roughly $1,625 per month at the stated overage rate. High-traffic real-time applications, such as chat or collaboration tools, typically need the Team plan specifically for its higher connection limits, which is a jump many teams underestimate when they budget off the Pro tier alone.

title: Supabase vs Postgres: when you don't need the extras (2026) - DEV Community
text:
Supabase vs Postgres: when you don't need the extras (2026) - DEV Community
octave Nkurunziza
Posted on Nov 10 • Edited on Nov 10 • Originally published at blog.hubfly.space
# Supabase vs Postgres: when you don't need the extras (2026)
*Last updated: 6 November 2026*
Supabase vs Postgres is a strange matchup, because Supabase *is* Postgres. What you're really deciding is whether to pay for the pieces Supabase puts around it: sign-in, file storage, live updates, an auto-generated API and backups. For some apps that bundle is the best $25 you'll spend. For others it's $25 a month for a database plus features you never call. This guide shows what each piece costs on its own, where Supabase clearly wins, and how to keep your Supabase-style security rules working on plain Postgres if you move.
**Try it on Hubfly space**: a managed PostgreSQL 18 database starts at about $2 a month.
Prices are as of 6 November 2026, in US dollars.
## What Supabase adds on top of Postgres
Every Supabase project is a regular Postgres database. Around it, Supabase runs several services and gives them one dashboard, one client library and one bill.
|Supabase piece|What it does for you|Plain-Postgres replacement|
|Auth|Sign-up, login, OAuth, magic links; puts the user ID in every request|An auth library in your API (e.g. Better Auth or Auth.js), or a hosted service like Clerk |
|Auto-generated API|Query tables straight from the browser, guarded by row-level security|Your own small API (Express, FastAPI, Go…)|
|Row-level security helpers|`auth.uid()` inside policies|The same policies, plus a 10-line shim (below)|
|Storage|Files in buckets with access rules|Any S3-compatible bucket|
|Realtime|Live updates over WebSockets|A Pusher-compatible server, or Postgres `LISTEN/NOTIFY` in your API|
|Edge Functions|Server code next to the database|Code in your API container|
|Backups|Daily backups on paid plans, optional point-in-time restore|Managed backups from your provider, or scheduled `pg\_dump`|
The pattern is clear: Supabase's extras replace code you would otherwise write and run. That's the trade. You pay less for plain Postgres, and you write (or wire up) more yourself.
## Supabase pricing in 2026
From Supabase's pricing page:
* **Free: $0.** 500 MB database, 50,000 monthly active users, 1 GB of files, 5 GB of egress, 2 active projects. No automatic backups. Projects are paused after 1 week of inactivity.
* **Pro: from $25/month.** Includes $10 of compute credit, which covers one Micro instance (shared CPU, 1 GB RAM). 8 GB of disk, 100,000 monthly active users, 100 GB of files, 250 GB of egress, daily backups kept 7 days.
* **Team: from $599/month.**
Pro overage rates: disk $0.125/GB, users $0.00325 each past 100,000, files $0.0213/GB, egress $0.09/GB ($0.03 cached). Point-in-time restore is an add-on at $100/month for 7 days, and a custom domain is $10/month. Bigger compute costs extra: Small (2 GB) about $15, Medium (4 GB) about $60.
## Plain Postgres pricing in 2026
Here is what a database alone costs, roughly matched to Supabase Pro's 1 GB Micro instance.
|Provider|Smallest sensible plan|Monthly price|Backups|
|Supabase Pro|Micro, 1 GB RAM, 8 GB disk|$25 (includes auth, files, realtime)|Daily, 7 days|
|Neon Launch|Usage-based, billed per compute-hour|Neon's own example: about $15 for 140 compute-hours and 1 GB|Instant restore, $0.20/GB-month|
|Render|1 GB RAM|$19 + storage at $0.30/GB|Point-in-time restore, 3 days (Hobby) or 7 days (Pro)|
|DigitalOcean|1 vCPU, 1 GiB|$15.15 with 10 GiB|Daily backups + 7-day point-in-time restore|
|Hubfly space|Small, 0.5 vCPU, 1 GiB, 10 GiB|$3.92|No automatic backups yet (coming soon)|
Two things stand out. Supabase Pro is a fair price once you count everything in it. And if you only need the database, you can pay a fraction of that.
Neon deserves a special mention: every plan now includes managed Better Auth, a Data API and Realtime at no separate charge, with auth for up to 60,000 monthly active users per project on Free and 1 million on paid plans. If what you want is "Postgres plus login", it's a strong middle ground.
## Supabase vs Postgres: same app, two bills
Take a typical small SaaS: a 2 GB database, 10,000 monthly active users, 20 GB of uploaded files and live updates in the UI.
**On Supabase Pro: $25.00 a month.** Everything fits inside Pro's included amounts: 2 GB of the 8 GB disk, 10,000 of 100,000 users, 20 GB of 100 GB of files. The free plan won't do, because the database alone is over its 500 MB limit.
**On plain Postgres plus your own pieces (Hubfly space): $9.09 a month.**
|Piece|Size|Monthly|
|Hubfly space managed PostgreSQL|Small: 0.5 vCPU, 1 GiB, 10 GiB|$3.92|
|Hubfly space Cell container (runs your auth library and API)|0.5 vCPU, 1 GB, 10 GB disk, always on|$3.03|
|Hubfly space Storage|20 GB of files|$0.22|
|Managed Realtime|Nano|$1.92|
|Auth|Open-source library inside your API|$0|
|**Total**||**$9.09**|
How each number is worked out (730 hours a month; CPU $0.004 per vCPU-hour, memory $0.002 per GB-hour, storage $0.00001536 per GB-hour):
* **Database:** (0.5 × $0.004 + 1 × $0.002) = $0.004/h, plus the 30% management fee ($0.0012/h), plus 11 GiB of disk (10 GiB data + 1 GiB system) × $0.00001536 = $0.000169/h. Total $0.005369/h × 730 = **$3.92**.
* **API container:** (0.5 × $0.004 + 1 × $0.002) × 730 = $2.92, plus 10 GB × $0.00001536 × 730 = $0.11. Total **$3.03**.
* **Files:** 20 GB × $0.00001536 × 730 = **$0.22**.
* **Realtime:** the Nano size is $1.92, with no per-message fee.
Network transfer isn't in either total. Supabase Pro includes 250 GB of egress; check your provider's bandwidth terms before comparing heavy-download apps.
### When the math flips
The gap closes fast if you'd buy auth as a hosted service. Say the app grows to 150,000 monthly active users:
* **Supabase Pro:** $25 + 50,000 extra users × $0.00325 = **$187.50**.
* **Clerk Pro** (billed monthly) for sign-in alone, assuming all 150,000 count as Clerk's monthly retained users: $25 + 50,000 users × $0.02 + 50,000 users × $0.018 = **$1,925**.
* **An open-source auth library** in your own API: $0 extra, but you own password resets, OAuth setup and security updates.
So Supabase's included users are a big deal if your alternative is a hosted auth service. They matter much less if you're happy running a library yourself.
## When Supabase is the better choice
Be honest about what you'd rebuild. Pick Supabase when:
* **You'd otherwise buy hosted auth.** 100,000 monthly active users are included in Pro.
* **Your app is mostly frontend.** The auto-generated API plus row-level security means many apps need no backend server at all.
* **You want backups handled.** Pro keeps 7 days of daily backups without you doing anything, and point-in-time restore is available as a $100/month add-on.
* **You're prototyping.** The free plan gets you a database, login and file uploads in minutes. Just remember free projects pause after a week without activity.
* **You value one dashboard.** One place for users, tables, files, logs and keys saves real time on a small team.
## When plain Postgres is the better choice
* **You already have a backend.** If your API handles auth and business logic, Supabase's auto-generated API goes unused.
* **You only need a database.** A 1 GB managed Postgres costs $3.92 to about $20 elsewhere versus $25.
* **You want to own your auth data.** Users live in your own tables, with no provider-specific schema.
The honest downside on Hubfly space today: managed Postgres runs on a single node, with no replicas, no high availability and no point-in-time restore, and automatic backups are still coming. Until they arrive, run your own `pg\_dump` on a schedule from any machine or job runner you already have, and keep the files somewhere else (the dump and restore commands are in how to upgrade Postgres to a new major version in Docker). If you need automatic backups or failover today, Supabase Pro, DigitalOcean or Render are the safer picks.
## Moving from Supabase to plain Postgres: the part guides skip
Most migration guides say "run `pg\_dump`, then `pg\_restore`". On a typical Supabase schema, that fails, because your tables and policies point at things that only exist inside Supabase: the `auth` schema, the `auth.uid()` function and roles such as `authenticated`.
Here's a typical table from a Supabase app:
```
create table public.todos (
  id bigint generated by default as identity primary key,
  user_id uuid not null default auth.uid() references auth.users(id) on delete cascade,
  title text not null,
  done boolean not null default false

...

alter table public.todos enable row level security;
create policy "own todos read" on public.todos
  for select to authenticated using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
create policy "own todos write" on public.todos
  for insert to authenticated with check ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
